name: Rhinoplasty tip-narrowing sutures

lead: Tip-narrowing sutures give a broad or bulbous nasal tip a slimmer, more refined shape. The stitches reshape the cartilage rather than cutting it away, so the tip is narrowed while the tissue stays in place.

Sutures placed in the lower lateral cartilages pull and hold the folded cartilage in a tighter shape, narrowing the tip, and the change shows once swelling settles. General rhinoplasty references describe sutures as a standard way to narrow a wide tip; little published research has looked at the technique on its own.

paras: It is performed by a surgeon as one step within a rhinoplasty, often alongside other tip or bridge work. The nose is swollen at first, and the narrower tip becomes clear as healing progresses over the following months.
Risks are those of rhinoplasty in general, including revision surgery in roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations. It is a surgical procedure performed under anesthesia.

angle.text: People with a broad or bulbous nasal tip get stitches that reshape and narrow the tip cartilage without removing it, giving a slimmer, more refined nose. The change is visible once healing is complete. Little dedicated research on the technique alone has been published.

lead: Tip-narrowing sutures are stitches placed in the lower lateral cartilages of the nose during rhinoplasty to reshape and narrow a broad or bulbous tip without removing cartilage. For people who want a more defined, refined nose tip, the technique offers a way to slim the tip and sharpen its contours from within, rather than by cutting cartilage away. General rhinoplasty references describe sutures as a way to narrow a wide tip by tightening the folded cartilage apex [1].

Reviews describe suture techniques as remodelling the tip by changing the configuration of the tip cartilages and their supporting structures while preserving anatomy and limiting resection; effects are visible during surgery and can be adjusted or reversed, and one review concludes that sutures should be considered instead of tissue excision whenever possible [2]. A 2016 overview of the broad, bulbous tip says earlier reductive techniques produced unnatural results over time, and presents suturing and structural grafting as the contemporary approach [3].

The named sutures in a modern surgeon's repertoire include the medial crural, middle crural, interdomal, transdomal, lateral crural, medial crural anchor, tip rotation, medial crural footplate and lateral crural convexity control sutures [4]. Published work is mostly review articles and surgeon technique descriptions; no randomised trial of tip sutures alone was found.

Because the tip is the most prominent part of the nose, its width, rotation and definition strongly shape how the whole nose reads in a face photo or profile [5]. Tip sutures are one of the tools surgeons use to slim a wide tip, and they are usually combined with other steps in a single rhinoplasty plan.

paras: Surgeons can narrow the tip by suturing the cartilage rather than resecting it, and open rhinoplasty is described as giving better visualization and precision for tip work [1]. Suture work is often combined with grafts such as the columellar strut. A video-based review of tip shaping emphasises that nasal tip anatomy has a large effect on the overall look of the nose and focuses on tip sutures and cartilage grafts in open rhinoplasty [6]. Techniques have also been adapted to closed rhinoplasty, for example a septocolumellar loop suture between the medial crura and caudal septum [7].

The external shape of the tip is determined by the curves and contours of the lower lateral cartilages and by how they interact with the surrounding tissue; a review of nasal tip grafts notes that normative data exist for the ideal shape and shadowing of the tip [5]. Reviews of the broad, bulbous tip describe the goal as a refined but properly narrowed domal region with graceful contours that continue sideways to the alar lobule, with natural-looking shadowing [3].

Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article adds that thick skin can mask the cartilage framework and may call for more aggressive tip definition, and that tip support can be rebuilt with a columellar strut or a septal extension graft, the latter described as giving greater control and less change over time [1].

Reviews describe a family of sutures, each acting on a different part of the cartilage: medial crural, middle crural, interdomal, transdomal, lateral crural, medial crural anchor, tip rotation, medial crural footplate and lateral crural convexity control sutures [4]. Narrowing comes mainly from sutures that fold and tighten the domes, while others change rotation or projection. One review presents common techniques, suture algorithms and the indications and side effects of each [2].

Sutures are often paired with structural grafts. Reviews list the commonly used tip grafts as the floating graft, tip onlay, columellar strut, caudal septal extension, shield, alar batten onlay and lateral crural strut grafts, among others [5]. Authors describe the combination of suturing and grafting as the contemporary approach to a wide tip, replacing earlier reductive methods that were found to give unnatural results over time [3].

Open rhinoplasty is described as giving better visualization and precision for tip work [1]. Closed approaches have also been adapted, for example a septocolumellar loop suture between the medial crura and caudal septum [7]. Wikipedia reports that systematic reviews found no significant long-term difference in functional or satisfaction scores between open and closed approaches, and that surgeon expertise and anatomy mainly guide the choice [1].

Suture techniques for reshaping the tip have been used for many decades, with the last two decades before 2003 the most influential in shaping current methods. Early tip techniques sacrificed the integrity of the lateral crus to gain projection, which could disrupt tip support and lead to supratip fullness, asymmetry, tip drop or an overoperated look. Modern tip surgery is built on using sutures to directly reshape and reposition tip components rather than merely secure excised cartilage [4].

A review of tip sutures notes they are powerful enough that they must be performed precisely to avoid creating cosmetic as well as functional problems [8]. Risks are those of rhinoplasty in general; revision surgery accounts for roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations, with pinched or asymmetric tips among reasons cited [1].

A systematic review and survey of Canadian and US plastic surgery residents concluded that rhinoplasty skills are learned largely through hands-on exposure, which remains a training challenge [9]. Video-based teaching resources on tip analysis, sutures and grafts have been published to supplement this [6].

No studies found for tip-narrowing sutures alone. Registered trials of related tip surgery include a study of lateral crural steal with a columellar strut (NCT07317947, 22 participants, recruiting) [10] and a comparison of septal advancement flap and columellar strut effect on the tip (NCT06370455, 30 participants, completed) [11]. A 2025 report examined long-term outcomes of primary rhinoplasty more broadly [12].

timeline.event: John Orlando Roe performs the first modern endonasal rhinoplasty, for saddle nose [1].
Aurel Rethi introduces an open approach with a septal incision to modify the tip [1].
Maurice Cottle advocates the closed approach [1].
A. Sercer describes a columellar open approach; Padovan and later Wilfred Goodman (late 1970s) popularize open rhinoplasty [1].
A review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery traces the evolution of the major nasal tip suture techniques.[4]
Reviews summarise suture algorithms and conclude sutures should be preferred over tissue excision where possible.[2]
Overview of broad and bulbous tip reshaping presents suturing and structural grafting as the contemporary approach.[3]
